newsitem.title: USA: Seldane fall from grace opens allergy drug market.
newsitem.headline: Seldane fall from grace opens allergy drug market.

text.p: A proposal by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to remove its imprimatur from Seldane, an antihistamine marketed by a Hoechst AG unit, could benefit a host of pharmaceutical rivals, including Schering-Plough Corp, analysts said.

The FDA announced earlier in the week it intended to withdraw its approval of Seldane, or terfenadine, and Seldane D, or terfenadine and pseudoephedrine, due to the risk of serious cardiac effects when the drug was not used properly.
If the drug is pulled from the market, Schering-Plough's Claritin, Pfizer Inc's Zyrtec and Sepracor Inc could grab share, analysts said.

"The primary beneficiaries are all the other companies in the industry trying to gobble up market share in that category," Carl Seiden, an analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein, said. "The most obvious is Schering Plough's Claritin."
David Maris, an analyst at Aros Securities, predicted Claritin would gain the "lion's share" of Seldane market share, possibly as much as 50 percent.
He raised his worldwide Claritin forecast by $75 million, from $1.49 billion to $1.57 billion for 1997, versus the $1.15 billion estimated for 1996.

Nor was an FDA retraction a devastating blow to Hoechst, analysts said. Hoechst was marketing a metabolite version of Seldane called Allegra, which had similar benefits without the risks. The FDA also said its decision was influenced by its recent approval of Allegra.
"Hoechst knew Seldane was vulnerable to generic competition, and was already trying to cannibalize Seldane sales with Allegra sales," Seiden said.

When a patient ingested Seldane, the drug was broken up into several metabolites which fought allergy symptoms, Alex Zisson, an analyst at Hambrecht & Quist said. Scientists isolated the most effective of these metabolites in Allegra.
Hoechst Marion Roussell said it forecast U.S. sales of $300 million for Seldane in 1996 versus $394 million in 1995.
It said the decline was due to continued competition from Claritin and other antihistamines which did not have terfenadine's side effects.
The company said on Monday it would not take Seldane off the market and would defend the drug against the FDA proposal.
Another beneficiary would be Sepracor Inc, which licensed one of the patents covering Allegra to Hoechst, analysts said.

Richard Silver, an analyst at Lehman Brothers, said in a note that Sepracor held a patent on Allegra and would receive an eight percent royalty on sales following expiration of Hoechst's composition of matter patent either in 1999 or 2001.
"Sepracor will benefit to the extent that the FDA decision speeds up the transition of Seldane business into Allegra business," Seiden said.
Pfizer's Zyrtec would be a competitor, although it could not call itself "non-sedating" on its label, analysts said.
"Zyrtec is labelled as 'less-sedating," Seiden said. "But Pfizer has compensated for this by positioning the drug as a little bit more potent. They are great marketers."
An FDA approval withdrawal would also hurt Johnson and Johnson's Hismanal antihistamine drug, which has showed some of Seldane's side effects, analysts said.
"But Hismanal is simply not that big a deal for Johnson and Johnson," Seiden said.
((--Mary Kelleher, New York newsdesk 212-859-1707))
